evidence: src/interceptors/redact-values-in-response/redact-values-in-response.interceptor.ts: RedactValuesInResponseInterceptor.intercept calls hasReadRestrictedAccessPermission({ impersonationId, user }) || isRestrictedView(user), then redactPaths({ object: data, paths: DEFAULT_REDACTED_PATHS }). The permission and redaction rules come from shared helpers and are not reimplemented here.

src/interceptors/redact-values-in-response/redact-values-in-response.module.ts: RedactValuesInResponseModule is an empty @Module({}) wrapper. It contains no logic of its own and doesn't compete with the interceptor.
Both files deal only with response redaction. Callers (account, activities, portfolio, user, and public controllers and their modules) use the interceptor and the module in matching pairs.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The module has one concern: redacting sensitive values in HTTP responses when the viewer has restricted access. The interceptor file holds all of the logic. It does not write its own permission check or redaction code. Instead it calls the shared helpers (hasReadRestrictedAccessPermission, isRestrictedView, redactPaths) and uses the shared DEFAULT_REDACTED_PATHS config, so the redaction rule lives in one place. The module file is an empty Nest @Module wrapper. That is a normal Nest pattern, because controllers attach interceptors directly with @UseInterceptors and don't need them injected as providers. Neither file repeats logic or works around the module's own abstractions. One small point: the empty module doesn't register or export the interceptor, but that is a framework-wiring style choice, not a split concern or a duplicated rule.
